15368.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse flesk (“pork, flesh”), from Proto-Germanic *flaiski (“meat, flesh”). The further origin is uncertain; the Proto-Germanic form has been connected with *pleh₁ḱ- (“to tear, peel off”) and with words denoting cut or split-off pieces, such as flís (“splinter, wood chip”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk flesk, Faroese flesk, Icelandic flesk and fleski, Danish flæsk and Swedish fläsk (“pork, bacon”), as well as English flesh, Dutch vlees and German Fleisch (“meat, flesh”).

106760.etyen:
Borrowed from English rib (“rib; projecting ridge or flange”), from Middle English ribbe (“rib”), from Old English ribb (“rib”), from Proto-West Germanic *ribi (“rib”), from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib”). The technical senses developed metaphorically from the anatomical rib, referring to a narrow projecting support, ridge or flange; the textile sense refers to fabric formed with raised ribs. Doublet of ribbe (“rib; raised ridge”) and rev (“reef”).
The English source is cognate with Dutch rib, German Rippe, Icelandic rif and Faroese riv (“rib; reef”).

17928.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian frænka (“kinswoman, female relative”), from Old Norse frænka (“kinswoman”), a contracted form of frændkona (“kinswoman”), itself formed from frændi (“kinsman, relative; friend”) and kona (“woman, wife”), literally “kinsman-woman”.
The first element frændi is from Proto-Germanic *frijōndz (“friend, loved one”), originally the present participle of Proto-Germanic *frijōną (“to love”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preyH- (“to please; love”). The second element kona is from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ (“woman, wife”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn (“woman”).
